title: Longitudinal Circulating Tumor DNA–Guided Resistance Analysis During Second-Line Osimertinib Treatment
author: JW Tijmen van der Wel; Merel Jebbink; Vincent van der Noort; Ferry Lalezari; Daan van den Broek; Gerrina Ruiter; Jacobus A Burgers; Paul Baas; Anne SR van Lindert; Eva E van der Wall; Lisanne EA Kastelijn; Marrit Vermeulen; Linda JW Bosch; Kim Monkhorst; Mirjam C Boelens; Egbert F Smit; Adrianus J de Langen
text:
Abstract
Introduction
In osimertinib-treated EGFR mutation (EGFRm)–positive NSCLC, resistance inevitably occurs. Early resistance mechanism (RM) detection by circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in plasma and consecutive targeted treatment may delay progressive disease (PD). In this multicenter prospective study, we evaluated the detection rate and time interval of RM emergence in plasma ctDNA before radiologic PD.
Methods
Patients with EGFRm–positive NSCLC, treated with second- or third-line osimertinib, underwent computed tomography of the thorax and ctDNA analysis (Roche AVENIO expanded panel, research use only [Roche Sequencing Solutions, Roche, Basel, Switzerland]) at baseline and every 8 weeks for response evaluation and EGFRm and RM detection. If MET amplification preceded PD, crizotinib was to be added to osimertinib. Other RMs were monitored but not acted on. After PD, patients underwent a tumor biopsy.
Results
Of the 21 evaluable patients, 18 had detectable ctDNA at baseline. In patients with undetectable ctDNA at baseline, ctDNA remained undetectable during treatment. In the 17 out of 18 (94%) patients with detectable ctDNA, PD occurred. In seven out of 21 patients (33%), the EGFRm variant allele frequency increase preceded radiologic PD with a median interval of 9 weeks (range 7–34). In seven out of 21 patients (33%), at least one RM was detected before PD, and the median interval was 14 weeks (range 7–34). Three had one or more RM in ctDNA at baseline. No MET amplification was observed, and treatment with crizotinib was not initiated in any patient. After PD, 16 biopsies were obtained. Five confirmed the RM detected in plasma, five biopsies revealed additional RMs, and six harbored no RM.
Conclusions
In 33% of patients treated with second- or third-line osimertinib, RMs in plasma preceded PD by a median of 14 weeks, suggesting an opportunity for early treatment adjustment, potentially extending tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment duration.
Keywords: EGFR, NSCLC, Osimertinib, Resistance, ctDNA
Introduction
Osimertinib is a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that was initially approved for EGFR mutation–positive (EGFRm+) patients who progressed on earlier-generation EGFR TKIs because of EGFR T790M mutation.1,2 Despite high response rates and long and deep responses, resistance to osimertinib and subsequent disease progression (PD) eventually occurs in every patient.
Given that the emergence of resistance mechanisms (RMs) precedes clinically detectable PD, these may be detectable before PD occurs.3,4 Early detection and elimination of a resistant clone might prevent subclonal resistance and spatial heterogeneity, thereby delaying radiologic and clinical progression.5, 6, 7, 8 MET amplification is one of the most common RMs to osimertinib9 and can be safely and effectively treated by adding a MET TKI (e.g. crizotinib) to osimertinib treatment.10, 11, 12
A plethora of mutations, copy number variations, fusions, and events such as histologic transformation may cause resistance to osimertinib,9 and many are detectable at the time of PD in plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).13,14
The primary aim of this study was to identify the percentage of patients in which an increase in circulating tumor DNA was detectable (increase in driver mutation variant allele frequency [VAF], emergence of an RM, or both) before radiologic PD. The secondary aim was to determine the success rate of crizotinib and osimertinib combination treatment to eliminate MET amplification, defined by the disappearance of the MET amplification clone in a subsequent ctDNA sample.
Study design
In this multicenter prospective study, patients with EGFRm+ (exon19 deletion with or without insertion, or L858R) NSCLC that developed EGFR T790M–mediated resistance (confirmed in tissue, plasma or both) on first or second generation EGFR TKI were treated with osimertinib 80mg daily (Table 1). Osimertinib was not a study treatment but was prescribed as a standard-of-care treatment. Patients were radiologically evaluated with computed tomography of the thorax, blood was drawn for next-generation sequencing (NGS) of ctDNA using the AVENIO ctDNA expanded panel (research use only [RUO]) and routine laboratory work. The response evaluation interval was once every 6 weeks for the first 6 months of the study and was adjusted to every 8 weeks thereafter. After 1 year of treatment with osimertinib, response evaluation frequency was decreased to once every 12 weeks depending on the patient’s and treating physician’s preference. Patients were treated with osimertinib until radiologic progression (Response evaluation criteria in solid tumors [RECIST] version 1.1) or unacceptable toxicity.

| Inclusion Criteria | Exclusion Criteria |
|---|---|
| Histologically confirmed metastatic NSCLC, characterized by a sensitizing exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R EGFR mutation. | Patients with symptomatic central nervous system metastases who are neurologically unstable. |

Initially, we aimed to include 30 patients in this study. On the basis of earlier reports,9 we expected that 30% of patients treated with osimertinib develop MET amplification-based resistance. With an assumed sensitivity of 70% for MET amplification detection in ctDNA, we expected to identify MET amplification in seven patients. However, the study was expanded to 100 patients and divided into a first and second- or third-line osimertinib cohort, the latter of which is described in this report.
All patients with a detectable RM in plasma continued osimertinib until radiologic progression, unless the RM was MET amplification. In that case, patients were to be treated with a combination of osimertinib and crizotinib (250 mg twice daily) until either disappearance of MET amplification in a subsequent plasma sample, radiologic or clinical PD, or unacceptable toxicity occurred.
When patients developed PD, a tumor biopsy of a progressive lesion was acquired for RM analysis using DNA and RNA NGS mutation analysis. The results of the tumor biopsy were then correlated to plasma sequencing results.
All patients provided written informed consent. The study protocol and informed consent form were approved by The Netherlands Cancer Institute’s Medical Ethics Assessment Committee (Dutch: Medisch-Ethische Toetsingscommissie, METC), and subsequent amendments. The study was carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and registered under ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT04148066.
Study Outcomes
The primary objective was to identify the percentage of patients in which an increase in ctDNA was detectable (increase in driver mutation VAF, emergence of an RM or both) before radiologic PD. RM detection was twofold: (1) a rise in driver mutation VAF, and (2) detection of a known genomically-defined RM.
Among the secondary objectives was the determination of the time interval between ctDNA-based detection of resistance and radiologic progression. Other secondary objectives were related to the detection and treatment of MET amplification. These include the determination of the success rate of crizotinib and osimertinib combination treatment to eliminate MET amplification and the time to reappearance of MET amplification as detected by ctDNA (or tumor biopsy of a progressive lesion in case of radiologic progression) after successful elimination with crizotinib treatment. A successful elimination was defined by the disappearance of the MET amplification clone in a subsequent ctDNA sample. The safety of this combination therapy in terms of Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.03 was also to be assessed.
Study Start and Response Evaluations
At the first outpatient clinic visit, medical history (histologic diagnosis, stage of cancer, EGFR mutation status in plasma and tumor biopsy, previous systemic treatment, start and stop date of last treatment) was taken, demographics (age, sex, smoking history) and a performance status according to the WHO criteria were assessed and informed consent was obtained. Blood was drawn for ctDNA analysis using AVENIO ctDNA expanded panel (RUO) and routine laboratory work. In addition, tumor assessment using appropriate radiologic techniques was performed and scored using RECIST 1.1. Osimertinib treatment was initiated after this first assessment.
Medical history, performance status assessment, blood analysis, and radiologic assessment were performed every 6 to 8 weeks for the first year, and every 12 weeks thereafter.
CtDNA Analysis
For plasma sequencing in patients treated at the Netherlands Cancer Institute (NKI), 20 mL of K2-EDTA was collected and processed within 2 hours using a two-step centrifugation protocol (20 min at 380xg to isolate the platelets, after which the supernatant was centrifuged for 10 min at 16,000xg to obtain cell-free plasma). For patients treated outside the NKI, 20 mL of blood was collected in STRECK BCT tubes (Streck, Inc., La Vista, NE) and sent to the NKI by postal service. Plasma isolation was then performed as described above, within 5 days after blood collection.
DNA isolation was performed using the Qiagen Symphony DSP Circulating DNA kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All samples were stored at −80°C until analysis. Library prep was performed using the AVENIO ctDNA expanded kit (RUO) according to the guidelines from the manufacturer. Sequencing was performed using the NextSeq HS550 (Illumina, San Diego, CA). Analysis was done through Roche AVENIO ctDNA analysis software (Roche Sequencing Solutions). In ctDNA analysis, variants were reported when VAF was at least 0.1%. Any increase in VAF between two subsequent plasma samples was regarded as ctDNA progression. For copy number variation (CNV) analysis, a CNV score of at least 5 combined with a genomic region of less than 20% of the affected chromosome was required for amplification calling, with a genomic region of less than 5% being interpreted as a probable amplification and genomic region greater than or equal to 5% but less than 20% as possible amplification. All variants were analyzed and classified by a clinical molecular scientist. Both “possible” and “probable” amplifications were regarded as amplifications in this analysis.
Information on handling MET amplification before PD and coverage of AVENIO’s Expanded Panel (RUO) and the DNA and RNA NGS panels used for the postprogression biopsy can be found as supplementary information.
Analyses
Statistical analysis was performed using R software version 4.4.0 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria). The number of patients with an RM before radiologic progression was calculated as a percentage of the total number of patients that developed PD.
The time interval between any increase in driver mutation VAF and radiologic progression was calculated as a median with range. The same was done for the time interval between ctDNA-based detection of an RM and radiologic progression.
A descriptive analysis was used for correlation between RMs detected in plasma before PD, RMs detected in plasma at the time of PD, and RMs detected in a tumor biopsy after PD.
Results
From July 2019 to July 2020, 25 patients were enrolled. A total of 22 were treated at the NKI, two at St. Antonius Hospital Nieuwegein, and one at Haaglanden Medical Center, The Hague.
Four patients were nonevaluable. One had a primary EGFR mutation that was not an exon 19 deletion (with or without insertion) or L858R mutation, one was not evaluable as they had passed away (without PD) before their first response evaluation, one was withdrawn from the study because of patient noncompliance, and one patient developed osimertinib-related pneumonitis 2 weeks after treatment initiation, and therefore, discontinued osimertinib treatment before the first response evaluation, leading to assessable survival data for 21 patients (Fig. 1, Table 2).

At the time of database lock (July 1, 2023), 17 of 21 evaluable patients had progressed on osimertinib, two patients had an ongoing response, one patient had developed osimertinib-related pneumonitis and discontinued osimertinib (after undergoing one response evaluation), and one patient died without PD because of coronavirus disease 2019. In total, 18 patients had died. A total of 16 of the evaluable patients had measurable disease (RECIST version 1.1) at baseline. No complete responses were observed, and a partial response was reached in four patients, resulting in an overall response rate of 25%. The median progression-free survival on osimertinib monotherapy was 5.0 months (95% confidence interval 3.1–6.9 mo), and the median overall survival was 22.1 months (95% confidence interval 20.2–23.9 mo).
Driver Mutation Detection
All patients had confirmed the presence of EGFR T790M in plasma, biopsy, or both before study inclusion. In the plasma sample obtained at baseline, the primary EGFR driver was detected in 18 out of 21 patients (85.7%), and in 14 out of 21 (66.7%) EGFR T790M was detected. None of the patients with undetectable ctDNA (VAF <0.10%) at baseline had detectable ctDNA during osimertinib treatment, nor at the time of PD (Fig. 2).
Of the 18 patients with detectable ctDNA at baseline, 17 developed radiologic PD; one patient had an ongoing response at the time of database lock.
In total, seven patients had detectable ctDNA at baseline and any measure of elevation of the driver mutation VAF before PD. The median interval between elevation of the primary EGFR driver VAF and PD was 9 weeks (range 7–34 wk). Four patients had detectable ctDNA at baseline and any measure of elevation at the time of, but not before, PD. Six patients exhibited no elevation of the primary driver VAF during osimertinib treatment, including at the time of radiologic PD, but did have detectable ctDNA at baseline. Three patients had no detectable ctDNA at any time point. The patient who died without PD died of a noncancer-related death. This patient had no detectable ctDNA at baseline, and no emergence of the driver VAF had occurred during osimertinib treatment.
All patients who developed ctDNA PD also developed radiologic PD.
RM Detection
Co-alterations leading to osimertinib resistance were detected in seven out of 21 (33.3%) patients before PD (BRAF V600E alone, BRAF V600E, and PIK3CA H1047L, ERBB2 amplification, ERBB2 L755P, EGFR amplification, EGFR C797S, EGFR G724S [n = 1 each]). In one patient, EGFR G724S emerged before PD. However, at the time of PD, EGFR C797S was also detected in plasma. In another patient, ERBB2 amplification was observed before PD, but at the time of PD, plasma sequencing identified ERBB2 L755S and an ALK fusion as well. Notably, no MET amplification was detected in any patient and, therefore, no therapeutic adjustments were made. The median interval from RM detection to PD was 14 weeks (range 7–34 wk) for the seven patients in which the RM was detected before PD. In three of these patients, the RM was already detected at baseline (BRAF V600E, EGFR amplification, ERBB2 amplification [all n = 1]). The median interval from RM detection to PD in patients with a detectable RM at baseline was 14 weeks (range 9–21 wk). For the four patients in whom the RM was first detected after initiating osimertinib treatment, the median interval was 16 weeks (range 7–34 wk). No RMs were detected in plasma samples from patients who did not develop PD (n = 3).
Six of the patients with RM detection exhibited elevation of the driver mutation VAF before PD. No RM was detected between the re-emergence of the primary driver mutation and PD in two patients.
Tumor Biopsy And ctDNA Results
A total of 16 patients, including the seven patients in which an RM was detected in ctDNA before radiologic progression, underwent a biopsy after radiologic progression. DNA and RNA NGS were performed on these samples. Results from plasma sequencing and tumor biopsy analysis were compared for patients in which an RM was detected in ctDNA before radiologic progression (n=7) (Table 3). The primary driver mutation was detected in all seven relevant tumor biopsies.

One tumor biopsy harbored no RMs. In one tumor biopsy a BRAF fusion was detected, which is not covered in the AVENIO expanded panel (RUO), whereas plasma sequencing identified a BRAF V600E mutation. Three of seven tumor biopsies were fully in agreement with plasma sequencing. These tumor biopsies harbored BRAF V600E and PIK3CA H1047L in one patient, EGFR C797S in one patient, and ERBB2 L755P in one patient. In one patient, ERBB2 amplification emerged before PD, but at the time of PD, an ALK fusion, and ERBB2 L755S were detected in plasma. The tumor biopsy harbored ERBB2 amplification and ERBB2 L755S, but no ALK fusion. Finally, one patient’s plasma sample initially identified EGFR G724S before PD, whereas at the time of PD, plasma sequencing identified EGFR G724S and EGFR C797S. In the tissue biopsy, only EGFR C797S was found, and no EGFR G724S. The two patients in whom re-emergence of the primary driver VAF without emergence of an RM was observed, also underwent tumor biopsy. Although the primary driver mutation was detected in both biopsies, no RM was identified in either biopsy.
Discussion
To our knowledge, this is the first trial in which broad serial ctDNA resistance analysis is performed during second or third-line osimertinib treatment in EGFRm+ NSCLC. Other published works on longitudinal ctDNA monitoring in patients treated with osimertinib used smaller panels. One study by Remon et al.15 solely monitored EGFR T790M, whereas a study from Watanabe et al.16 monitored EGFR exon 19 deletions and EGFR L858R, T790M, and C797S mutations. An earlier report, in which blood samples of patients treated with erlotinib were analyzed for the primary driver mutation and EGFR T790M, found that the RM could be identified 15 to 344 days before PD in nine patients.3
Detection of the (re)emergence of the oncogenic driver and the emergence of RMs before PD is possible in a selected group of patients with detectable ctDNA at the start of second-line osimertinib treatment. In the current cohort, the interval between identification of an RM and PD varied between 51 and 239 days. Using the strategy described here, we were able to identify the emergence of drug resistance (increase in driver VAF) in seven patients (33.3%), and an RM with ctDNA before radiologic progression in seven patients as well.
In two patients, no RM was detected between the re-emergence of the primary driver mutation and radiologic progression. Interestingly, no RM was identified in the tissue sample obtained after PD either. Possibly, this can be explained by an RM not covered in either the AVENIO expanded panel (RUO) or the utilized RNA and DNA NGS panels.
We described patients in whom, at the time of PD, detected RMs in plasma, and tissues differ from one another. This may be a result of disease heterogeneity, in which the biopsied lesion harbors different RMs than other progressive tumor lesions.17 Plasma sequencing identifies RMs from various progressive lesions, leading to a discrepancy between the two modalities.
On the basis of previous publications,9 we assumed an incidence of 30% for MET amplification as an RM to osimertinib. However, given that no MET amplification was detected in any patient before PD, we were unable to reach all study objectives, including the success rate, and safety of crizotinib and osimertinib combination treatment. Possibly, no MET amplification was detected because of the lower sensitivity of amplification detection with ctDNA. A technical validation study performed in our center revealed a concordance rate of 100% between the AVENIO Targeted Panel and droplet digital polymerase chain reaction regarding EGFR amplifications.18 We, therefore, assume that the lack of MET amplification detection was not on the basis of a technical error. CNV calls are susceptible to false-negative results because of low tumor content, more so than single-nucleotide variation calls.19 Therefore, smaller metastases harboring MET (or any other) amplification might not be detected by ctDNA analysis before radiologic progression has occurred. However, ctDNA analysis revealed ERBB2 amplification before progression in one patient, meaning amplifications can be identified before PD. No treatment intervention was initiated on the basis of this finding, however. A small number of patients developed resistance to osimertinib because of RNA-based RMs. An ALK fusion was detected in the plasma of one patient and a BRAF fusion was found in the tissue of another patient. As described previously, these RMs are observed less frequently than DNA-based RMs.9,20
In patients in which ctDNA was undetectable at baseline, no ctDNA was detected during treatment or at PD. This may be a result of low tumor burden in these patients, tumor site localization, a low proliferation index, or a combination of any of these factors.21, 22, 23 On the basis of our findings, the strategy explored in this study does not seem to be applicable to this group of patients. Two of three patients included in this study in which no ctDNA was detectable at baseline did not have measurable disease according to RECIST version 1.1, which may explain the absence of ctDNA.
A recent retrospective analysis by Gray et al.24 describes the emergence of ctDNA PD before RECIST-defined PD in patients receiving either first or second-line osimertinib and the emergence of RMs before radiologic PD. This analysis, however, because of its retrospective nature, does not include attempts to intervene when these RMs emerge. Future trials utilizing the strategy described in the study reported here may explore intervening when any targetable RM arises.
Of note, not all potential RMs are covered in the AVENIO expanded panel (RUO), potentially leading to an incomplete molecular evaluation. This is observed in one patient in which BRAF fusion was confirmed in the tissue biopsy.
Despite the fact that not all secondary study objectives were reached, important conclusions may be drawn from the results presented here.
AVENIO expanded panel (RUO) was able to detect an osimertinib-resistant clone through re-emergence of the driver mutation in plasma, without radiologic progression, in 33% of patients. Identification of an RM, with or without an increase in the primary driver mutation before radiologic progression was successful in 33% of patients. In two of these patients, additional RMs developed during treatment, suggesting an increase in disease heterogeneity during an ongoing radiologic response. This in turn alludes to a window of opportunity for targeted therapy adjustment between the emergence of an RM and radiologic progression. However, detection of the osimertinib-resistant clone in these seven patients required the sequencing of 108 plasma samples across the entire study population, suggesting that the approach explored here is most probably not cost-effective.
Another possible limitation for clinical implementation of the strategy we implemented is the turnaround time between blood drawing and definitive results of plasma sequencing: approximately 3 weeks.
An alternative approach, in which droplet digital polymerase chain reaction is used for driver mutation detection and expanded to a broader panel in case of a positive analysis would decrease the turnaround time for most response evaluations, in which the driver mutation is not detected, and dramatically decrease costs. This approach is currently being explored in a separate study of patients on first-line osimertinib.
The study reported here revealed that RMs may be detected before radiologic progression in seven of 21 patients treated with second-line osimertinib with a median of 14 weeks before radiologic progression. In most of these patients, the same RM is detected in a tumor biopsy at the time of radiologic progression. This suggests a window of opportunity for early treatment targeting osimertinib resistance and possibly delaying radiologic progression in a select group of patients.
